name: Software Supply-Chain Security
description: Security of dependencies, package registries, build systems, CI/CD, and code provenance.

ndss.narrative:
Supply-chain security at NDSS has grown from isolated case studies into a coherent field examining the trust chains that connect developers to deployed software. How Bad Can It Git? (NDSS 2019) characterized secret leakage in public GitHub repositories at scale, documenting the operational consequence of version-control hygiene failures. Automating Patching of Vulnerable Open-Source Software Versions in Android Apps (NDSS 2019) addressed the downstream propagation problem: vulnerabilities in shared libraries persist in app stores long after patches are available.

BreakApp (NDSS 2018) took an architectural approach, proposing automated compartmentalization to contain the damage from a compromised library. Towards Measuring Supply Chain Attacks on Package Managers (NDSS 2021) then provided the first systematic empirical study of how package repositories are targeted, revealing that typosquatting and dependency confusion are widespread.

The 2023–2025 papers show supply-chain risks penetrating developer tooling itself. BlockScope (NDSS 2023) detected vulnerabilities propagated into forked blockchain codebases through clone-tracking; UntrustIDE (NDSS 2024) exposed weaknesses in VS Code extensions that run with elevated privileges; and JBomAudit (NDSS 2025) assessed the landscape, compliance status, and security implications of Software Bills of Materials—reflecting the post-Log4Shell era's regulatory push for supply-chain transparency.

sp.narrative:
Supply-chain security at IEEE S&P emerged as a cohesive topic around 2020-2022 as high-profile incidents (SolarWinds, XZ Utils) moved it from niche concern to front-page threat. The early S&P papers were prescient: SPIDER: Enabling Fast Patch Propagation In Related Software Repositories (S&P 2020) addressed how security patches spread through dependency trees, and ICAS: an Extensible Framework for Estimating the Susceptibility of IC Layouts to Additive Trojans (S&P 2020) tackled hardware supply-chain trojan insertion.

The 2022-2023 cohort brought the package-registry and ML model supply chains to S&P. BadEncoder: Backdoor Attacks to Pre-trained Encoders in Self-Supervised Learning (S&P 2022) showed that poisoning the pre-training phase of a self-supervised encoder poisons all downstream models that fine-tune from it. SoK: Taxonomy of Attacks on Open-Source Software Supply Chains (S&P 2023) systematized the full attack landscape from typosquatting to maintainer account compromise. Committed to Trust: A Qualitative Study on Security and Trust in Open Source Software Projects (S&P 2022) examined the human and social factors governing who gets trusted to merge code.

Investigating Package Related Security Threats in Software Registries (S&P 2023) measured malicious package prevalence across npm, PyPI, and RubyGems. It's Like Flossing Your Teeth: On the Importance and Challenges of Reproducible Builds for Software Supply Chain Security (S&P 2023) assessed reproducible-build adoption as a supply-chain verification mechanism.

By 2024, AI-code-generation tools joined the supply chain. TrojanPuzzle: Covertly Poisoning Code-Suggestion Models (S&P 2024) and Poisoned ChatGPT Finds Work for Idle Hands (S&P 2024) showed that poisoning LLM training data or code-suggestion models inserts vulnerabilities into developer-written code, extending supply-chain attacks upstream into the AI toolchain.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this set framed software supply-chain security as an ecosystem-trust problem. "Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem" (USENIX 2019) mapped how a handful of maintainers and deeply nested transitive dependencies create outsized risk across npm, making the case that a single compromised package can ripple through thousands of downstream projects. In parallel, "in-toto: Providing farm-to-table guarantees for bits and bytes" (USENIX 2019) attacked the problem from the provenance side, proposing a cryptographic framework to attest that every step of the build pipeline was carried out by the right actor in the right order. Together these two set the field's twin agendas: measuring real-world ecosystem risk, and building verifiable trust into the supply chain.

The early 2020s broadened the threat surface from packages to the whole reuse-and-build stack. A cluster of work tackled vulnerability propagation through reused code: "V0Finder: Discovering the Correct Origin of Publicly Reported Software Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2021) traced where bugs actually originated, while "MOVERY" (USENIX 2022) and later "V1SCAN" (USENIX 2023) pushed precise detection of modified, cloned vulnerable components in C/C++. At the same time attention turned to CI/CD itself as an attack surface: "Characterizing the Security of Github CI Workflows" (USENIX 2022) and "ARGUS: A Framework for Staged Static Taint Analysis of GitHub Workflows and Actions" (USENIX 2023) showed that automated build and deploy pipelines were under-examined and exploitable. Registry-level deception also became a named research target with "Exploring the Unchartered Space of Container Registry Typosquatting" (USENIX 2022) and "Beyond Typosquatting: An In-depth Look at Package Confusion" (USENIX 2023), which systematized how developers get tricked into pulling the wrong artifact.

The most recent shift, from 2024 onward, is the entanglement of machine learning with the supply chain, in both directions. As offense, "An LLM-Assisted Easy-to-Trigger Backdoor Attack on Code Completion Models" (USENIX 2024), building on the earlier "You Autocomplete Me: Poisoning Vulnerabilities in Neural Code Completion" (USENIX 2021), showed that AI coding assistants are themselves a poisonable link in the chain. As defense, "DONAPI" (USENIX 2024) and "MalGuard" (USENIX 2025) apply behavior- and ML-based detection to catch malicious npm and PyPI packages at scale. The frontier work, "ChainFuzz: Exploiting Upstream Vulnerabilities in Open-Source Supply Chains" (USENIX 2025), closes a loop the field opened in 2019: rather than just measuring or detecting risk, it actively reasons about how upstream bugs become exploitable downstream. The trajectory runs from "this ecosystem is fragile" to fine-grained provenance, build-pipeline and registry hardening, and now AI-era attack and defense.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treated software reuse mainly as a question of how to safely contain untrusted third-party code and how to reason about the integrity of the build pipeline. BreakApp (NDSS 2018) argued for automatically compartmentalizing third-party modules so a single bad dependency could not compromise an entire application, while in-toto (USENIX 2019) introduced "farm-to-table" guarantees that cryptographically tie together every step from source commit to final artifact. Around the same time, empirical studies began mapping the scale of the problem: Small World with High Risks (USENIX 2019) showed how a handful of npm maintainers and transitively-pulled packages create enormous attack surface, and How Bad Can It Git? (NDSS 2019) documented rampant secret leakage in public GitHub repositories. Together these established the two enduring threads of the field: measure the ecosystem's exposure, and build mechanisms to harden it.

The next phase, roughly 2020-2022, deepened both threads. Qualitative and measurement work like A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management (CCS 2020) and Committed to Trust (S&P 2022) explained the human and organizational reasons developers ship vulnerable or untrusted dependencies, while Towards Using Source Code Repositories to Identify Software Supply Chain Attacks (CCS 2020) and Supply-Chain Vulnerability Elimination via Active Learning and Regeneration (CCS 2021) pushed toward detecting and removing malicious or vulnerable components. A second front opened around the infrastructure itself: Characterizing the Security of Github CI Workflows (USENIX 2022) exposed how CI/CD pipelines are themselves exploitable, and Exploring the Unchartered Space of Container Registry Typosquatting (USENIX 2022) showed registries beyond npm/PyPI are equally targetable. On the defensive side, Sigstore (CCS 2022) made artifact signing practical at ecosystem scale, directly responding to SolarWinds-era anxieties.

By 2023 the field had matured enough to consolidate and systematize. SoK: Taxonomy of Attacks on Open-Source Software Supply Chains (S&P 2023) gave the community a shared vocabulary for the attack surface, and several papers sharpened specific defenses: Beyond Typosquatting (USENIX 2023) characterized the broader "package confusion" class, Investigating Package Related Security Threats in Software Registries (S&P 2023) compared threats across registries, and "It's like flossing your teeth" (S&P 2023) elevated reproducible builds as a foundational provenance guarantee. A parallel strand on vulnerability propagation and clone detection (V1SCAN and MOVERY, USENIX 2022-2023; GraphSPD, S&P 2023) tackled how known bugs silently spread through reused C/C++ and Java code.

Most recently the center of gravity has shifted toward AI in the supply chain, on both ends. Attack papers like TrojanPuzzle (S&P 2024) and An LLM-Assisted Easy-to-Trigger Backdoor Attack on Code Completion Models (USENIX 2024) show that code-suggestion models and their training data are a new injection vector, complementing Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical (S&P 2024). At the same time, LLMs are being turned into defenders, as in DONAPI (USENIX 2024), which mines package behavior sequences to flag malicious npm packages. The arc thus runs from compartmentalizing and signing trusted code, through large-scale ecosystem measurement and registry/CI hardening, to a present in which the data and models that now write our code are themselves part of the supply chain to be attacked and defended.
